definition: The DARPA Agent Markup Language (DAML) was the name of a US funding program at the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) started in 1999 by then-Program Manager James Hendler, and later run by Murray Burke, Mark Greaves and Michael Pagels.
details: The program focused on the creation of machine-readable representations for the Web. One of the Investigators working on the program was Tim Berners-Lee. Working with the program managers and other participants, Tim helped shape the effort to create technologies and demonstrations for what is now called the Semantic Web, leading in turn to the growth of knowledge graph technology. A primary outcome of the DAML program was the DAML language, an agent markup language based on RDF. This language was followed by an extension entitled DAML+OIL which included researchers outside of the DARPA program in the design. The 2002 submission of the DAML+OIL language to the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) captures the work done by DAML contractors and the EU/U.S. ad hoc Joint Committee on Agent Markup Languages. This submission was the starting point for the language (later called OWL) to be developed by W3C's web ontology working group, WebOnt. DAML+OIL was a syntax, layered on RDF and XML, that could be used to describe sets of facts making up an ontology. explainer.lead: DAML was an effort to give web information meanings that computers could read, not just text that people could read. Its language work fed into DAML+OIL and then OWL, helping lay groundwork for the Semantic Web and knowledge graphs.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a class where everyone uses the same labels in their notebooks, such as “person,” “place,” and “works at.” A computer can then understand facts from different notebooks without guessing what each label means. DAML helped create shared labels and rules like these for the web.
tiers.practitioner: Treat DAML primarily as a historical predecessor in ontology engineering: DAML used RDF, while DAML+OIL provided an RDF- and XML-layered syntax for ontology facts. Its 2002 W3C submission became the starting point for WebOnt’s work on OWL. A key pitfall is treating DAML+OIL and OWL as interchangeable, or confusing the DAML language with the DARPA funding program.
tiers.paperLevel: DAML was an RDF-based agent markup language, and DAML+OIL was a syntax layered on RDF and XML for describing sets of facts constituting an ontology. DAML+OIL drew on DAML, OIL (Ontology Inference Layer), and SHOE. The 2002 W3C submission represented work by DAML contractors and the EU/U.S. ad hoc Joint Committee on Agent Markup Languages, and initiated the standards work that produced OWL.

explainer.example: An ontology could identify “Ada Lovelace” as a “Person” and “London” as a “Place,” using shared categories expressed as machine-readable facts. Software reading another entry with those same categories would not have to treat the labels as meaningless strings.

explainer.intuition: Ordinary web text tells people what something says, but not necessarily what its labels and relationships mean. DAML aimed to express those meanings in a machine-readable form so that web facts could be shared through a common ontology.
howItWorks: DARPA funded work on machine-readable representations for the Web.
Researchers developed DAML, an agent markup language based on RDF.
DAML was extended through DAML+OIL, with roots in DAML, OIL, and SHOE.
DAML+OIL described ontology facts using a syntax layered on RDF and XML.
Its 2002 W3C submission became the starting point for OWL.
explainer.whyItMatters: DAML connected DARPA-funded research with the standards process that produced OWL. That lineage helped move machine-readable web ontologies from research demonstrations toward broader Semantic Web and knowledge graph work.
misconceptions: DAML was both a DARPA funding program and the name of a language produced by that program.
DAML+OIL was not simply another name for OWL; it was a starting point for OWL’s development.
DAML concerned machine-readable meaning and ontology facts, not the visual formatting of web pages.
